entry: Expectations of the end of the present age, human history, or the world. Several world religions predict that negative events will reach a climax at the end of the world. Belief that the end is imminent, known as apocalypticism, has been held by members of mainstream religions and by doomsday cults. The Abrahamic religions maintain a linear cosmology with themes of transformation and redemption. In [[Judaism]], "end of days" refers to the Messianic Age. In [[Christianity]], a period of tribulation precedes the second coming of Christ, who will face the [[Antichrist]]. In [[Islam]], hadiths describe events before the Day of Judgment, including the emergence of the Mahdi. Indian religions tend to be cyclical. In [[Hinduism]], [[Kalki]], the final incarnation of Vishnu, ends the [[Kali Yuga]]. Since the 18th-century development of the concept of deep time, scientific discourse has considered the ultimate fate of the universe, including the [[Big Crunch]] and the Big Freeze (heat death).

Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium of the genus *Escherichia*, commonly found in the lower intestine of warm-blooded animals. Most strains are part of the normal gut microbiota and are harmless or beneficial to their hosts, some producing vitamin K2 and preventing colonization by harmful bacteria. Certain serotypes, such as EPEC and ETEC, are [[Pathogen|pathogenic]] and cause serious food poisoning. Fecal–oral transmission is the major route of disease. Because cells survive outside the body for a limited time, the bacterium is used as an indicator organism for fecal contamination in environmental samples. *E. coli* is the most widely studied prokaryotic [[Model organism|model organism]] and has served as the host for most [[DNA|recombinant DNA]] work. It has been intensively investigated for over 60 years, and under favorable conditions it can reproduce in as little as 20 minutes.

Language family of the Arctic and subarctic. Native to northern North America and a small part of northeastern Asia, the family has two branches: the Eskimoan languages, comprising Inuit and Yupik, and the Aleut branch, which consists of the single Aleut language. Inuit languages are spoken across northern [[Alaska]], Canada and [[Greenland]], and Yupik languages in western and southwestern Alaska and Chukotka. The family has no proven genetic relationship to any other language family. The Alaska Native Language Center estimates that the ancestral language divided into the Eskimoan and Aleut branches at least 4,000 years ago. Proposed external relationships include the Eskimo–[[Uralic languages|Uralic]] hypothesis, suggested by Danish linguist Rasmus Rask in 1818, and Michael Fortescue's Uralo–Siberian hypothesis, published in 1998. Both remain unproven.

[[Vertebrate|Vertebrate]] organ, a fibromuscular tube through which food passes from the pharynx to the [[Stomach|stomach]]. Also called the gullet, it is about 25 cm (10 in) long in adult humans. It runs behind the trachea and [[Heart|heart]], passes through the diaphragm, and empties into the upper stomach. Peristaltic contractions move food along, and the epiglottis tilts backward during swallowing to protect the larynx and lungs. Two muscular sphincters guard its ends, and the lower one helps prevent reflux of acidic stomach contents. Gastric reflux, cancer, varices, tears, constrictions and motility disorders can affect it. Diseases may cause difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), chest pain or no symptoms at all. Clinical investigation includes [[X-ray|X-rays]] with barium sulfate, [[Endoscopy|endoscopy]] and [[CT scan|CT scans]].

Constructed auxiliary language intended as a neutral second language for international communication. Created by L. L. Zamenhof and first published in 1887 under the pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto, it is the most successful constructed international auxiliary language and the only one with a sizeable population of native speakers, estimated at 2,000. Its vocabulary derives mostly from [[Romance languages]], with elements from Germanic, Greek and [[Slavic languages|Slavic]] languages. Its extensive system of prefixes and suffixes allows words to be combined freely. Estimates of total speakers vary, but two put the number of Esperantists at around 100,000. Speakers are concentrated in [[Europe]], [[East Asia]] and [[South America]]. No country has adopted it officially, although "Esperantujo", meaning Esperanto land, is used for the places where it is spoken. The language has faced suppression under authoritarian regimes.

Clandestine acquisition of secret or confidential information, also called spying or intelligence gathering. Espionage is often part of an institutional effort by a government or commercial concern, and the term is frequently associated with state spying on enemies for military purposes. Industrial espionage targets businesses. Spies may infiltrate an [[Military|military]] organization, return information on enemy forces, recruit collaborators and dissidents, or steal technology. Counterespionage, or counterintelligence, aims to thwart enemy espionage. The oldest known classified document was a report by a spy disguised as a diplomatic envoy at the court of King [[Hammurabi]]. *The Art of War* identifies five types of spies, including doomed spies used to spread disinformation. Espionage may be a legal tool of law enforcement or illegal and punishable by law, and almost all [[Sovereign state|sovereign states]] have laws concerning it.

Organized competition using [[Video game|video games]], usually between professional players in multiplayer events. Multiplayer competitions were largely amateur until the late 2000s and early 2010s, when online streaming platforms, particularly [[YouTube]] and [[Twitch (service)|Twitch]], enabled a surge in professional participation and spectators. Esports first became popular in [[East Asia]], particularly [[China]] and [[South Korea]], which first licensed professional players in 2000. Japan's broad anti-gambling laws prohibit prize pools for professional gaming tournaments. The most common genres are multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA), first-person shooter (FPS), fighting games and real-time strategy (RTS). The [[League of Legends World Championship]] is among the most popular tournaments. Although the legitimacy of esports as a true sport remains in question, the International Olympic Committee has discussed its inclusion, and an Olympic Esports Games is planned for 2027.

Written work giving the author's own argument, often reflecting a personal point of view. The definition is vague, and the form overlaps with letters, papers, articles, pamphlets and [[Short story|short stories]]. Formal essays have serious purpose and logical organization, while informal essays feature the personal element, humor and rambling structure. Essays are used for [[Literary criticism|literary criticism]], political manifestos, observations of daily life and reflection. Almost all modern essays are in [[Prose|prose]], though [[Alexander Pope]] wrote verse essays such as *An Essay on Criticism*. The word derives from the French *essayer*, "to try". [[Michel de Montaigne]] was the first author to describe his work as essays, meaning attempts to put his thoughts into writing. In the [[United States|United States]] and [[Canada]], essays are a major part of formal [[Education|education]], and universities use admission essays to select applicants. The concept extends to film essays and photographic essays.

Ceremonial county (pop., 2024: 1,929,610) in eastern England. Low-lying, with a flat coastline on the [[North Sea]] and the Thames Estuary, the county borders [[Greater London]] to the south-west. The [[Iron Age]] Trinovantes tribe established a settlement at Colchester, the oldest recorded town in Britain. Saxons later formed the Kingdom of Essex, and in 1381 the county's populace was heavily involved in the [[Peasants' Revolt]].

American businesswoman who co-founded a cosmetics company with her husband, Joseph Lauter (later Lauder). Born Josephine Esther Mentzer in Corona, Queens, [[New York City]], to Hungarian Jewish immigrants, she worked in her family's hardware store and later sold the creams of her uncle, a chemist, to beauty salons and resorts. In 1946 she and her husband launched the Estée Lauder Cosmetic Co. in New York. Her first fragrance, Youth-Dew, a bath oil that doubled as a [[Perfume|perfume]], was introduced in 1953 and became a bestseller. She pioneered the gift with purchase promotion and free samples, and emphasized in-store customer service. The company later added men's lines and allergen-free brands such as Clinique. Lauder was the only woman on [[Time (magazine)|Time magazine]]'s 1998 list of the 20 most influential business geniuses of the 20th century.

Compound derived from an acid in which the hydrogen of an acidic hydroxyl group is replaced by an organyl group. Esters are formed in a substitution reaction between a [[Carboxylic acid|carboxylic acid]] and an [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]]. Glycerides, which are [[Fatty acid|fatty acid]] esters of [[Glycerol|glycerol]], make up the bulk of animal fats and [[Vegetable oil|vegetable oils]]. Lactones, which are cyclic esters, contribute to the aroma of fruits, butter and celery. Low-molecular-weight esters usually have a pleasant smell and are used as fragrances. [[Polyester|Polyesters]] are important plastics, and esters of phosphoric acid form the backbone of [[DNA]] molecules. Esters of nitric acid, such as [[Nitroglycerin]], are known for their explosive properties. The word was coined in 1848 by German chemist Leopold Gmelin, probably as a contraction of the German *Essigäther*, "acetic ether".

Republic in the Baltic region of Northern Europe. It is bordered by [[Latvia]] to the south and [[Russia]] to the east, with the Gulf of Finland to the north and the [[Baltic Sea]] to the west. Its capital, [[Tallinn]], and Tartu are its largest urban areas, and Estonian is the first language of most of its nearly 1.4 million people. The medieval population was among the last pagan peoples in Europe to adopt [[Christianity]], after the Northern Crusades of the 13th century. After centuries of foreign rule, Estonia declared independence in 1918. It was occupied and annexed into the Soviet Union during [[World War II]], and full independence was restored on 20 August 1991 after the Singing Revolution. Estonia joined [[NATO]] and the [[European Union]] in 2004. It is a developed, high-income economy that ranks highly in international rankings for education and online public services.

Category of steroid sex hormones that regulate the female reproductive system and secondary sex characteristics. The three major endogenous estrogens are estrone (E1), estradiol (E2) and estriol (E3); estradiol is the most potent and prevalent. Estetrol (E4) is produced only during pregnancy. Estrogens bind to estrogen receptors inside cells, which modulate the expression of many genes, and also activate membrane receptors such as GPER. They are synthesized from [[Testosterone|testosterone]] and other androgens by the [[Enzyme|enzyme]] aromatase. Estrogens are used as medications in [[Menopause|menopausal]] hormone therapy and hormonal birth control. Synthetic and natural estrogens found in the environment, known as xenoestrogens, are among the endocrine-disrupting compounds that can cause reproductive dysfunction in wildlife and humans. In both sexes, circulating levels of estrogen are lower than those of androgens.

Partially enclosed coastal body of brackish water where freshwater and saltwater mix. Estuaries are transition zones between riverine and marine environments, classified as ecotones. Their conditions are shaped by [[Tide|tides]], waves, saline intrusion, freshwater flow and sediment input. The mixing of seawater and freshwater provides high levels of nutrients, making estuaries among the most productive natural habitats in the world. Most existing estuaries formed in the [[Holocene]] epoch, when rising seas flooded river-eroded or glacially scoured valleys about 10,000–12,000 years ago. Many are called bays, harbors, [[Lagoon|lagoons]], inlets or sounds. The word derives from the Latin *aestuarium*, "tidal inlet of the sea", from *aestus*, meaning tide. Soil erosion, deforestation, overfishing, the filling of wetlands, and pollutants such as heavy metals and [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbons]] degrade many estuaries.

Landlocked kingdom in Southern Africa, formerly Swaziland. It is bordered by [[South Africa]] on all sides except the east, where it borders [[Mozambique]], and is the second smallest country in continental Africa. The executive capital is Mbabane, and the legislative capital is Lobamba. The Swazi established their kingdom in the mid-18th century under Ngwane III, and the country and the Swazi take their names from Mswati II, who expanded and unified it. After the Second Boer War it was a British high commission territory from 1903 until independence on 6 September 1968. In April 2018 the king changed the official name to Kingdom of Eswatini. Eswatini is an [[Absolute monarchy|absolute monarchy]], the last of its kind in Africa, and political parties are prohibited from running in elections. [[HIV/AIDS]] and [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]] are widespread, and 28% of adults are HIV-positive. Critics attribute persistent poverty and inequality to centralized power.

headword: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind
sort_key: eternal sunshine of the spotless mind
entry: 2004 American [[Science fiction|science fiction]] romantic drama film directed by Michel Gondry. [[Jim Carrey]] and [[Kate Winslet]] star as a couple who undergo memory erasure after they break up, in a nonlinear narrative about memory and love. The title is taken from *Eloisa to Abelard*, an 1717 poem by [[Alexander Pope]]. The film grossed $72.9 million on a $20 million budget. At the 77th Academy Awards it won Best Original Screenplay, and it has gained a cult following.

Naturally occurring organic compound (C₂H₆), a colorless, odorless gas at [[Standard temperature and pressure|standard temperature and pressure]]. It makes up 1–6% of [[Natural gas|natural gas]] by volume, second only to [[Methane|methane]], and is isolated from natural gas and as a by-product of petroleum refining. Its chief use is as [[Ethylene|ethylene]] feedstock. In 1834 [[Michael Faraday]] first synthesized it by electrolysis of potassium acetate solution, mistaking the product for methane. Ethane was discovered dissolved in Pennsylvanian light crude oil by Edmund Ronalds in 1864. Its boiling point is −88.5 °C. The molecule adopts a staggered conformation, and the barrier to rotating its methyl groups is 12 kJ/mol (2.9 kcal/mol). The ethyl group is formally, though rarely in practice, derived from ethane.

Volatile, flammable alcohol (CH₃CH₂OH) that is the active ingredient in alcoholic beverages. A central nervous system depressant, it is the second most consumed drug globally, behind [[Caffeine|caffeine]]. It is produced by yeast [[Fermentation|fermentation]] of sugars or by [[Ethylene|ethylene]] hydration. Historically used as a general anesthetic, it is now used as an antiseptic, disinfectant and solvent for some medications, and as an antidote for [[Methanol|methanol]] and [[Ethylene glycol|ethylene glycol]] poisoning. It is also a fuel for lamps, stoves and internal combustion engines. As of 2024, world production of ethanol fuel was 120 gigaliters, mostly from the U.S. (51%) and [[Brazil]] (30%). The name was officially adopted in 1892 at a nomenclature conference in [[Geneva]], while *alcohol* originally described a powdered cosmetic.

Class of organic compounds in which an oxygen atom is bonded to two organyl groups, R–O–R′. Ethers are common in [[Organic chemistry|organic chemistry]] and especially in biochemistry, where they link [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]] and lignin. Symmetrical ethers have the same organyl group on both sides of the oxygen, while mixed ethers differ. [[Diethyl ether|Diethyl ether]], the solvent and anesthetic commonly called simply "ether", is a typical symmetrical example. Ethers feature bent C–O–C linkages, with the oxygen sp³ hybridized. Polyethers contain ether linkages in their main chain, and crown ethers are cyclic polyethers. Certain toxins produced by [[Dinoflagellate|dinoflagellates]], such as palytoxin, are large cyclic or ladder polyethers. Compounds such as [[Ester|esters]] have C–O–C linkages but are not considered ethers. Ethers were first isolated by Pierre-François-Guillaume Boullay and his son in the early 19th century.

Family of wired [[Computer network|computer networking]] standards designed for local area networks. Commercially introduced in 1980 and first standardized in 1983 as IEEE 802.3, it is an open standard that has largely replaced competing wired LAN technologies such as Token Ring and FDDI. Early Ethernet used a shared coaxial cable, while modern variants use twisted pair and fiber optic links with switches. Data rates have grown from the original 2.94 Mbit/s to 800 Gbit/s, with 1.6 Tbit/s under development. Systems divide data into frames carrying source and destination addresses and error-checking data. Robert Metcalfe named the network in 1973 to emphasize that it could run over any transmission medium. Its 48-bit MAC address was adopted by IEEE 802.11, known as [[Wi-Fi]]. Ethernet commonly carries [[Internet Protocol|Internet Protocol]] traffic and is one of the key technologies of the [[Internet]].

Civil war in Ethiopia and present-day [[Eritrea]], 1974–1991. It was fought between the [[Derg]], a military junta, and Ethiopian and Eritrean rebel groups. The Derg overthrew Emperor [[Haile Selassie]] in a coup on 12 September 1974 and established a communist state. Rebel fronts, including the Eritrean People's Liberation Front and the Tigrayan People's Liberation Front, had already been fighting the imperial regime. The Derg used counterinsurgency campaigns and the Red Terror to repress them. In 1977 Somalia invaded to back rebels in the Ogaden, prompting a large Soviet and Cuban intervention. Famine in 1983–1985 and economic decline increased support for the rebels. The Derg dissolved its military junta in 1987 and became civilianized, but it was overwhelmed by rebel groups. The war ended on 28 May 1991, when rebels entered [[Addis Ababa]] and President Mengistu Haile Mariam fled to [[Zimbabwe]]. At least 1.4 million people died, 1 million of them in famine-related deaths.

Country in the Horn of Africa (1270–1974), historically known as Abyssinia. Founded by Yekuno Amlak, who claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, the Solomonic dynasty replaced the Agaw kingdom of the Zagwe. Amda Seyon I and Dawit I expanded it into the dominant force in the Horn of Africa, and it reached its peak under [[Zara Yaqob|Zara Yaqob]] (r. 1434–1468). Emperor Fasilides founded [[Gondar]] in the 1630s, beginning a golden age. After a period of decentralization known as the Zemene Mesafint, Emperor Tewodros II reunified the empire. Emperor [[Menelik II]] expanded it to its modern boundaries and defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, preserving independence. Italy occupied the empire during World War II until it was driven out with British help. Emperor [[Haile Selassie]] returned from exile, and the empire became a founding member of the [[United Nations]]. The 1973 Wollo famine and domestic discontent led to the 1974 coup by the Derg.

Rugged mountain mass in northeastern Africa, extending from [[Ethiopia|Ethiopia]] into [[Eritrea|Eritrea]]. Known as the "Roof of Africa", it is the largest continuous area of its elevation on the continent, with little of its surface below 1,500 m and summits up to 4,550 m. The Great East African Rift System bisects it diagonally. The highlands are divided by the Main Ethiopian Rift into the northwestern Abyssinian Massif, which contains Ras Dashen (4,550 m), Ethiopia's highest peak, and the southeastern Harar Massif, home to the Bale Mountains. Lake Tana, source of the [[Blue Nile|Blue Nile]], lies in the northwest. Most of the country's major cities, including [[Addis Ababa|Addis Ababa]], are at elevations of about 2,000–2,500 m. The highlands began rising 75 million years ago, and a flood basalt plateau formed around 30 million years ago. The former Kingdom of Kaffa, in the southern highlands, was the point from which the [[Coffee|coffee]] plant was exported to the [[Arabian Peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]].

Largest of the [[Oriental Orthodox Churches|Oriental Orthodox]] churches, and the first indigenous Christian church from sub-Saharan Africa. Christianity was introduced to the [[Kingdom of Aksum|Kingdom of Aksum]] by Coptic Orthodox missionaries in 330. The church was administratively part of the [[Coptic Orthodox Church|Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria]] until it was granted autocephaly, with its own patriarch, in 1959. It has between 38 million and 51 million adherents in [[Ethiopia|Ethiopia]] and 60 million members worldwide, and it is a founding member of the World Council of Churches. Its name, *Tewahedo*, is a Ge'ez word meaning "united as one", referring to the miaphysite belief in one united nature of Christ. Around 500 bishops refused to accept the two-natures doctrine decreed by the Council of Chalcedon in 451.

Conflict between two or more ethnic groups in which the individuals involved expressly fight for their group's position within society. Political, social, economic or religious sources may underlie it. Academic explanations fall into three schools: primordialist, instrumentalist and constructivist. Primordialists argue that ethnic groups rest on kinship and primordial ties such as territorial location, a view associated with [[Clifford Geertz|Clifford Geertz]]. Other political scientists argue that institutional, political and economic factors cause conflicts, and that the concept of ethnic war is misleading. Primordial accounts struggle to explain why ethnic violence occurs in sporadic outbursts. Scholars debate whether ethnic conflict has become more prevalent since the end of the [[Cold War|Cold War]]. Management approaches include consociationalism and [[Federalism|federalism]]. Although [[Yugoslav Wars|Yugoslavia]] broke up in ethnic violence in the 1990s, it had enjoyed decades of peace before the Soviet Union collapsed.
